title: What is JSON?
summary: Explains JSON (JavaScript Object Notation) as the string format APIs use to send data, how it differs from a JS object, and how JSON.stringify and JSON.parse convert between the two. Ends with the Taco Town exercise: parse a recipe JSON string in an Express POST route and render the chosen recipe in EJS.

concepts.heading: What JSON is
points: JSON = JavaScript Object Notation: a text format for sending data over the internet that is both human-readable and compact. It is the usual format of API responses.
Its structure mirrors a JS object: key/value pairs separated by colons, comma-separated properties, arrays, and objects nested inside objects.
It is good at representing complex nested data (e.g. a person with an array of degrees, each degree an object).

concepts.heading: JSON vs a JavaScript object
points: Layout is almost identical, but in JSON every key must be a double-quoted string. JS object keys do not need quotes.
Values can be strings, numbers, arrays, objects (and booleans/null).

The real difference: JSON is serialized, meaning it is one single string, usually because it is travelling across a network. A JS object is a live in-memory structure that the interpreter understands and that has relaxed syntax.
Analogy: a JS object is the assembled wardrobe, JSON is the flat-pack box. Same content, minimal size for transport, re-assembled at the destination.
(Extra) Real JSON also forbids comments, trailing commas, single quotes and functions/undefined values; a JS object may contain all of those.

concepts.heading: Reading JSON: use a viewer
points: Raw API JSON is usually minified onto one line, which is hard for humans to read.
Paste it into a JSON visualiser (recommended: jsonviewer.stack.hu, free) and open the Viewer tab to expand/collapse nested nodes.
In the taco example the viewer shows an array of three recipe objects; each has ingredients -> protein, salsa and a toppings array of objects.
Viewer icons distinguish objects from arrays, which matters when deciding whether to drill with dot notation or loop.

concepts.heading: JSON.stringify and JSON.parse
points: JSON.stringify(obj) serializes: turns a JS object into a JSON string, keeping all the quotes, colons and commas that encode the nesting. Use it before sending data out.
JSON.parse(jsonString) is the reverse: turns the JSON string back into a normal JS object (or array).
After parsing you use ordinary property access, e.g. data.ingredients, indexing like data[0], loops, and so on.
(Extra) JSON.parse throws a SyntaxError on invalid JSON, so wrap it in try/catch when the source is untrusted.

concepts.heading: Taco Town exercise: how the pieces connect
points: index.js holds recipeJSON as one long string constant (standing in for a response from a third-party API, to avoid real requests for now). recipe.json has the same data pretty-printed for reference.
The page has a form posting to /recipe with three buttons that share name="choice" and have values chicken, beef, fish.
body-parser (urlencoded) makes the choice available as req.body.choice.
A switch on req.body.choice selects index 0, 1 or 2 of the parsed array.
The solution stores the pick in a variable, then redirects to GET /, which renders solution.ejs passing it as recipe.
In EJS: if recipe exists show recipe.name and the ingredients, otherwise show a prompt h2. Drill down with recipe.ingredients.protein.name, .preparation, recipe.ingredients.salsa.name.
toppings is an array of objects, so loop over it (forEach) and print quantity and name per li.

code_examples.caption: Serialize and parse
code_examples.code:
const wardrobe = { doors: 2, drawers: 3, color: "oak" };
const flat = JSON.stringify(wardrobe); // '{"doors":2,"drawers":3,"color":"oak"}'
const back = JSON.parse(flat);         // object again
console.log(back.doors);               // 2

task.name: Taco Town
task.starting_point: Starter folder with index.js (recipeJSON string, express, body-parser, empty POST /recipe), views/index.ejs, public/styles/main.css, recipe.json, solution.js and solution.ejs. Run npm install first.
task.goal: Make the site behave like the solution: clicking a chicken/beef/fish button shows that taco's name and ingredient list; before any click it shows a prompt.
steps: cd into the project folder and run npm install, then run nodemon solution.js and open localhost:3000 to see the target behaviour. Do not read solution.js or solution.ejs.
Study the JSON structure (recipe.json or a JSON viewer): array of 3 recipes, each with ingredients.protein, ingredients.salsa, ingredients.toppings[].
In the app.post("/recipe") handler, read req.body.choice.
Parse recipeJSON with JSON.parse and choose the matching element (switch or lookup) for chicken, beef, fish.
Send the chosen recipe to the template (res.render with data, or store it and redirect to /).
In views/index.ejs, show an h2 prompt if no data exists; otherwise show the recipe name.
List protein name and preparation, the salsa name, and loop over toppings to output quantity + name as list items.
task.expected_result: Initial page shows a 'pick your favourite taco' prompt; clicking an emoji button shows the recipe title and a ul such as 'Chicken, Grilled', 'Tomato Salsa', '1 cup of Lettuce', and so on.
task.reference_repo_path: Section 28 - Aplication Programming Interfaces (APIs)/28.03 - What is JSON

pitfalls: Forgetting to JSON.parse the string: indexing the string with [0] gives one character, not a recipe.
Using locals.recipe in EJS guards against a ReferenceError when the variable was never passed (first visit).
toppings is an array: use a loop, not dot notation. Protein and salsa are plain objects: use dot notation.
The reference solution keeps the choice in a module-level variable, so it is shared by all visitors; fine for a demo, wrong for real apps.
The reference repo's own index.ejs variant renders directly from the POST route (no redirect), so a refresh re-submits the form; the redirect pattern avoids that.
(Extra) Do not confuse JS object literal syntax with JSON: single quotes or unquoted keys make JSON.parse fail.

gaps_and_ideas: New lesson 'What is JSON?' with blurb: JSON is a string; stringify/parse convert it to and from objects.

Tasks: (1) stringify an object and log typeof; (2) parse a given JSON string and read a nested value; (3) fix an invalid JSON string (single quotes, trailing comma) until JSON.parse succeeds; (4) loop over a toppings array to build list items; (5) wrap parse in try/catch.
Starter code: a minified recipe JSON string constant plus an empty render function.
Interactive demo: two textareas, left JS object, right JSON string, with Stringify/Parse buttons and an error readout for invalid input, plus a collapsible tree view of the parsed result.
